passages.text: Knowing how to teach, Freire says, means creating the conditions for students to build and produce knowledge, not just playing a game of handing it over. Walk into the room open to questions and to students' curiosities, and to their hesitations too.

passages.ref: Pedagogy of Freedom, ch. 3, 'Knowing How to Listen'
passages.text: Teaching isn't passing your understanding to a student; it's provoking them to understand and to say what they've understood. That's why Freire felt obliged to listen to students' doubts, fears and struggles. It's in listening to a student that you learn how to speak with them.

passages.ref: Pedagogy of Freedom, ch. 3, 'Caring for the Students'
passages.text: Freire rejected the idea that the colder, more distant and grayer a teacher is, the better. Feeling isn't the enemy of knowing, as long as it doesn't bend your fairness. He found that the more rigorous he became, the more joyful and hopeful too. Joy doesn't only come when you find what you were looking for; it comes in the search.

passages.ref: Pedagogy of Freedom, ch. 2 (the child in the airport)
passages.text: Freire and his wife were stuck waiting for a red-eye flight, exhausted and sorry they hadn't changed their plans. What settled them was a small boy running around the departure lounge, announcing with delight that the plane was coming, and then that it had already landed. On a tired day, a child's curiosity can be the thing that brings you back.

passages.ref: Pedagogy of Freedom, ch. 2, 'Joy and Hope'
passages.text: Freire claimed a right to be angry, and to use that anger to fuel the struggle, just as he had a right to love. Just anger only makes sense because the future isn't fixed. Your anger at what's unfair isn't a flaw; it can be a sign you still believe things can change.

howard_thurman.label: Howard Thurman
howard_thurman.bio: Theologian, writer, and educator whose work joined spiritual depth with vocation, courage, and human dignity.

passages.text: Don't ask what the world needs. Ask what makes you come alive, and go do it.
There is something in every one of you that waits and listens for the sound of the genuine in yourself.

bell_hooks.label: bell hooks
bell_hooks.work: Teaching to Transgress; Teaching Community; Teaching Critical Thinking; All About Love
bell_hooks.bio: American author, professor, and cultural critic (born Gloria Jean Watkins) whose teaching trilogy and writing on love joined education, freedom, and community.

passages.ref: Teaching to Transgress, Introduction 'Teaching to Transgress' (p. 12)
passages.text: For all its limits, the classroom is still the most radical place of possibility we have.
passages.verbatim: The classroom remains the most radical space of possibility in the academy.

passages.ref: Teaching to Transgress, Introduction 'Teaching to Transgress' (pp. 2–3)
passages.text: At her all-Black grade school, Booker T. Washington, hooks was taught by Black women who saw nurturing young minds as resistance. School was sheer joy, a place where she could reinvent herself through ideas. After integration, she learned that what was wanted from her was obedience, not eagerness to learn.

passages.ref: Teaching to Transgress, Introduction 'Teaching to Transgress' (p. 7)
passages.text: The first idea that shaped her teaching was that the classroom should be exciting, never boring, and if boredom set in, the teacher should step in and change the atmosphere.

passages.ref: Teaching to Transgress, Introduction 'Teaching to Transgress' (p. 8)
passages.text: Excitement about ideas isn't enough. A class's ability to come alive depends on how much its members care about one another and hear one another.
passages.verbatim: our capacity to generate excitement is deeply affected by our interest in one another, in hearing one another’s voices, in recognizing one another’s presence.

passages.ref: Teaching to Transgress, Introduction 'Teaching to Transgress' (p. 8)
passages.text: Everyone shapes the classroom and everyone contributes, and those contributions are resources. The teacher has to really value each person's presence, and show it, not just say it.

Teaching is easiest for those who believe part of the vocation is sacred: the work isn't just passing on information but sharing in students' intellectual and spiritual growth, and caring for their souls.

Engaged pedagogy puts well-being at the center, including the teacher's. If you want to empower students you have to be committed to your own healing and growth; hooks draws on Thich Nhat Hanh's point that an unhappy helper can't help many people.
Students want to be seen as whole people with complicated lives, not just as collectors of bits of information, and teachers should want the same for themselves.

A holistic classroom is a place where teachers grow too. That can't happen if we refuse to be vulnerable while asking students to take risks; hooks never asked students to take a risk she wouldn't take herself.

passages.ref: Teaching to Transgress, ch. 14 'Ecstasy: Teaching and Learning Without Limits' (p. 207)
passages.text: The academy isn't paradise, but learning can be a place where paradise is made. With all its limits, the classroom is still a place of possibility, where we can face reality and imagine beyond it.
passages.verbatim: The classroom, with all its limitations, remains a location of possibility.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Preface 'Teaching and Living in Hope' (p. xiv)
passages.text: When we only name the problem and complain, without any constructive focus on what could change, we take away hope. Critique without hope turns into cynicism.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 2 'Time Out: Classrooms without Boundaries' (p. 14)
passages.text: hooks admits teacher burnout is real. Teachers need to be totally present to teach well, and when they can't be, the teaching suffers, so time away from the classroom isn't a luxury but a need.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 2 'Time Out' and publisher description
passages.text: Teaching doesn't only happen in classrooms. hooks found it liberating to teach in churches, bookstores, and homes, and to remember that learning goes wherever people gather.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 11 'Heart to Heart: Teaching with Love' (p. 127)
passages.text: Talking about love in teaching is almost taboo. Professing love for a subject is praised, but talk about loving students and people warn you not to get too close. hooks was criticized her whole career for being too emotional.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 11 'Heart to Heart: Teaching with Love' (p. 131)
passages.text: Love in the classroom has the same core as any love: care, commitment, knowledge, responsibility, respect, and trust. When those are there, teacher and student both end up learning.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 11 'Heart to Heart: Teaching with Love' (pp. 130–131)
passages.text: Competition breaks connection. When students are taught to see one another as rivals for the title of smartest, community can't form; a partnership model makes room for love.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 11 'Heart to Heart: Teaching with Love' (p. 136)
passages.text: In a class reading James Baldwin, some students had to face their own homophobia. hooks kept the room a learning community by insisting on respect and responsibility. Not everyone changed, but they learned to think past the small boundaries of their hatred, and that is where change begins.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 11 'Heart to Heart: Teaching with Love' (pp. 136–137)
passages.text: hooks asked a former student, now a law professor, whether loving her students had created favoritism. The student laughed: the more hooks loved them, the harder they had to work. There is no love without justice.

passages.ref: Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope, Teach 11 'Heart to Heart: Teaching with Love' (p. 137)
passages.text: Love in the classroom moves us away from domination. It always challenges us and changes us.
passages.verbatim: Love will always challenge and change us.

passages.ref: Teaching Critical Thinking: Practical Wisdom, Teaching 1 'Critical Thinking' (p. 8)
passages.text: Children are born critical thinkers, endlessly asking who, what, when, where and why. Too often their passion for thinking ends when they meet a world that wants only conformity and obedience.
passages.verbatim: Children are organically predisposed to be critical thinkers.

passages.ref: Teaching Critical Thinking: Practical Wisdom, Teaching 1 'Critical Thinking' (p. 7)
passages.text: Thinking is an action. The heartbeat of critical thinking is the longing to know how life works, and students first have to rediscover the joy and power of thinking itself.

passages.ref: Teaching Critical Thinking: Practical Wisdom, Teaching 1 'Critical Thinking' (p. 10)
passages.text: hooks calls for radical openness. Instead of assuming teachers must be right at all times, teachers should be open at all times and willing to say what they don't know.

passages.ref: Teaching Critical Thinking: Practical Wisdom, Teaching 1 'Critical Thinking' (p. 10)
passages.text: Most students resist critical thinking because passive learning is more comfortable, and teachers who push for it often get discouraged. It's usually the few, not the many, who learn it, and when they do it's deeply rewarding for both.

passages.ref: All About Love: New Visions, ch. 1 'Clarity: Give Love Words' (pp. 4–5)
passages.text: We'd love better if we used love as a verb. hooks takes M. Scott Peck's definition, the will to extend yourself to nurture your own or another's spiritual growth: love is a choice and an action, not just a feeling.

passages.ref: All About Love: New Visions, ch. 1 'Clarity: Give Love Words' (pp. 5–6)
passages.text: Affection is only one ingredient of love. Real love mixes care, affection, recognition, respect, commitment, trust, and honest, open communication. Feeling strongly drawn to someone isn't the same as loving them.

heschel.label: Abraham Joshua Heschel
heschel.work: The Sabbath; God in Search of Man; The Insecurity of Freedom
heschel.bio: Warsaw-born descendant of Hasidic rebbes who taught at the Jewish Theological Seminary and became one of the great American Jewish theologians. He wrote about wonder, holiness in time, and education, and marched with Dr. King at Selma.

passages.ref: The Sabbath (1951), "A Palace in Time," pp. 14–15
passages.text: Heschel called the Sabbath a palace in time that we build. We cannot build it out of stone; we build it out of hours we set apart, and then we get to live inside it.
Heschel said Judaism is a religion of time, aiming at making time holy. Our great cathedrals are our Sabbaths, and our holiest shrine is a day, Yom Kippur, which no army has ever been able to burn.
Six days a week we live under the pressure of things, of space. On the Sabbath we try to tune ourselves to holiness in time, turning from the results of creation to the mystery of creation.
All week, Heschel wrote, the spirit is left alone and forgotten; working under strain and worry, we have no mind for its beauty. But it waits for us to come and join it.

passages.ref: God in Search of Man (1955), ch. 5, p. 45
passages.text: Heschel called wonder, or radical amazement, the chief mark of a religious person's way of seeing nature and history: refusing to take the world for granted.

passages.ref: God in Search of Man (1955), ch. 5, p. 46
passages.text: For the philosophers, wonder is where knowledge starts and it ends once the cause is explained. For Heschel, wonder goes beyond knowledge and never ends; there is no answer in the world that dissolves our radical amazement. That is worth protecting in a classroom.

passages.ref: God in Search of Man (1955), ch. 5, p. 46
passages.text: Heschel wrote that humanity will not perish for lack of information, only for lack of appreciation, and that what we lack is not a will to believe but a will to wonder.
passages.verbatim: What we lack is not a will to believe but a will to wonder.

passages.ref: God in Search of Man (1955), "A Leap of Action"
passages.text: Where Kierkegaard spoke of a leap of faith, Heschel spoke of a leap of action: we come to understand by doing. The sacred deed itself is where a person meets God, even before every question is settled.

passages.ref: Heschel's written reflection after the Selma-to-Montgomery march, March 1965 (Heschel papers, Duke Rubenstein Library)
passages.text: After marching from Selma with Dr. King, Heschel wrote that even without words the march was worship: I felt my legs were praying. (It is often misquoted as praying with his feet.)
passages.verbatim: I felt my legs were praying.

passages.ref: "The Spirit of Jewish Education" (Jewish Education, Fall 1953); reprinted as "Jewish Education" in The Insecurity of Freedom, p. 237
passages.text: What we need more than anything else is not textbooks but text-people. (Heschel's point is about teachers, not against books.)
passages.verbatim: What we need more than anything else is not text-books but text-people.

passages.ref: "The Spirit of Jewish Education" (1953); "Jewish Education" in The Insecurity of Freedom
passages.text: The text students read most closely is the teacher: how you carry yourself, what you love, how you treat them. Heschel said that is the text they never forget.
passages.verbatim: It is the personality of the teacher which is the text that the pupils read; the text that they will never forget.

passages.text: Heschel, a lifelong teacher, admitted that he knew facts and techniques but had never learned how to kindle a spark. The spark is the real goal, and even the greats feel they have not mastered it.

We teachers face each pupil as an individual, with rights and tasks of their own. To educate is to meet the child's inner needs, and Heschel warned against sacrificing the individual child on the altar of the group.

Heschel asked whether what we teach will stay alive in a student's adult years, in bitter trials and disappointments, because all our lives we draw on the inspiration we received in childhood. Today's lesson may be what someone leans on decades from now.
What we must keep learning, Heschel said, is how to rise a little bit above ourselves, how to be a little holy for the sake of our own souls. Not perfect; a little higher than yesterday.

We cannot express the name of God in words, but we can express it in deeds. Heschel urged teaching mitzvot, deeds that train the tongue and senses to live by the soul's insight, rather than empty customs and ceremonies.

passages.ref: "Idols in the Temples," The Insecurity of Freedom (1966), p. 66
passages.text: Faith is not a formula, and it is never an arrival; it is always being on the way. It takes an instant to trust an idol and a lifetime of effort, prayer and selfless deeds to grow real attachment, and it comes with discovering that you are needed.

passages.ref: "Idols in the Temples," The Insecurity of Freedom (1966), p. 68
passages.text: Heschel named two goals of Jewish education: learning and sensitivity. Without sensitivity a person cannot deny themselves for others; without learning they cannot be truly pious. A good day in class builds both.

passages.ref: "The Values of Jewish Education," Proceedings of the Rabbinical Assembly 26 (1962), as quoted in Kaplan, Spiritual Radical (2007), p. 206
passages.text: Heschel said he had been a melamed, a teacher, all his life and knew how hard it is to teach: the first moment of every class is like standing at the Red Sea, waiting for it to part.
passages.note: Verbatim cleared 2026-11-27: wording reached only second- or third-hand.

passages.ref: "Children and Youth," The Insecurity of Freedom (1966), p. 44
passages.text: Self-respect is the fruit of discipline. Heschel taught that a young person's sense of dignity grows with the ability to say no to oneself, which is a gift we can help students build, not just a rule we impose.

passages.ref: "Teaching Religion to American Jews" (1956), in Moral Grandeur and Spiritual Audacity, p. 150
passages.text: Judaism treats learning as something close to worship. A person is not asked how much they know, Heschel said, but how much they learn, which applies to the teacher as much as the student.

passages.ref: Interview with Carl Stern, NBC, 1972 (in Moral Grandeur and Spiritual Audacity)
passages.text: In his last interview, Heschel's message to young people was that there is meaning beyond absurdity, that every little deed counts and every word has power, and that the meaning of life is to build it as if it were a work of art.

hillel.label: Hillel
hillel.bio: Hillel the Elder came from Babylonia as a poor student and became Nasi of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem. The Talmud remembers him for patience, humility and love of people, and the law follows his school. This guide draws on Talmud, Tosefta and Midrash; his sayings in Pirkei Avot belong to the pirkei_avot guide.

passages.text: Two men bet four hundred zuz on who could make Hillel lose his temper. On a Friday afternoon, while Hillel was washing his hair, one kept calling 'Who here is Hillel?' and asking insulting questions. Each time Hillel wrapped himself, came out, and said 'Ask, my son, ask.'
passages.verbatim: Hillel wrapped himself in a dignified garment and went out to greet him. He said to him: My son, what do you seek?

passages.text: When the man finally admitted he'd lost his bet, Hillel told him: Watch your temper. Hillel is worth losing four hundred zuz over, and another four hundred, and Hillel will not get angry.
passages.verbatim: Be vigilant of your spirit and avoid situations of this sort. Hillel is worthy of having you lose four hundred zuz and another four hundred zuz on his account, and Hillel will not get upset.

passages.text: A person should always be patient like Hillel, and not impatient like Shammai.
passages.verbatim: A person should always be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai.

passages.text: A man asked Shammai to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, and Shammai pushed him away with a builder's measuring stick. Hillel took him in and answered, then sent him off to keep learning.
What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn.
passages.verbatim: That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.

passages.text: A man would accept only the written Torah. Hillel taught him alef, bet, gimmel, dalet, then the next day taught the letters in a different order. When the man objected, Hillel said: you relied on me for the letters, so rely on me for the rest. He taught trust by building it first.
passages.verbatim: You see that it is impossible to learn what is written without relying on an oral tradition. Didn’t you rely on me?

passages.text: A man wanted to convert only so he could become High Priest. Instead of arguing, Hillel sent him to study the 'royal protocols.' Reading the Torah, the man worked it out for himself and dropped the demand. Hillel let the learning do the correcting.
passages.verbatim: Go and learn the royal protocols by engaging in Torah study.

passages.text: Years later, the three converts met and said: Shammai's impatience tried to drive us from the world; Hillel's patience brought us under the wings of the Divine Presence.
passages.verbatim: Shammai’s impatience sought to drive us from the world; Hillel’s patience brought us beneath the wings of the Divine Presence.

passages.text: In the Avot de-Rabbi Natan telling, when a skeptic came to Hillel, Shammai had already sent him away angrily. Hillel's first words were 'My son, take a seat.' He sat him down, then taught. Sitting someone down is often the beginning of the lesson.

Hillel earned half a dinar a day and gave half to the doorkeeper of the study hall. One day he had no work and was turned away, so he climbed to the roof and lay by the skylight to hear Shemaya and Avtalyon. Snow fell on him all night. At dawn they found him buried under it, warmed him, and said he was worth breaking Shabbat for.
passages.verbatim: He ascended to the roof, suspended himself, and sat at the edge of the skylight in order to hear the words of the Torah of the living God

passages.text: The Talmud says Hillel's poverty 'obligates the poor': no one can say they were too poor or too stretched to learn. It isn't a scolding; it means that whatever little room you have is enough to start.
passages.verbatim: Hillel obligates the poor

passages.text: Shammai spent the whole week setting aside the best food for Shabbat. Hillel had a different way: 'Blessed is the Lord day by day.' He trusted each day to bring its own blessing, so every ordinary act could be for the sake of Heaven.
passages.verbatim: all his actions, including those on a weekday, were for the sake of Heaven

passages.text: Hillel told his students he was going to do a mitzvah: bathe at the bathhouse. If the caretakers of kings' statues are honored for washing them, how much more should I care for my body, made in God's image? Taking care of yourself is holy work.
passages.verbatim: I who was created in the likeness and image [of God], as it is written: “For in the image of God, He made man” (Genesis 9:6), all the more so.

passages.text: Another time Hillel said he was going home to do a kindness for his guest. 'You have a guest every day?' His soul, he said, is a guest in the body: here today, maybe gone tomorrow. He treated tending his own inner life as hospitality.
passages.verbatim: And is this wretched soul not a guest inside the body; one day it is here, the next day it is not here.

passages.text: Dancing at the water-drawing celebration, Hillel said: If I am here, everyone is here; if I am not here, who is here? The Talmud reads it as: act as though it depends on you, and don't wait for others.
passages.verbatim: If I am here, everyone is here; and if I am not here, who is here?

passages.text: To the place that I love, there my feet take me. And God says: if you come to My house, I will come to yours.
passages.verbatim: To the place that I love, there my feet take me

passages.text: Both schools spoke words of the living God, yet the law follows Beit Hillel, because they were kind and humble. They taught Shammai's opinion along with their own, and even taught Shammai's first.
passages.verbatim: they were agreeable and forbearing, showing restraint when affronted, and when they taught the halakha they would teach both their own statements and the statements of Beit Shammai.

passages.text: After three years of dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, a heavenly voice declared: These and these are the words of the living God.
passages.verbatim: Both these and those are the words of the living God.

passages.text: Hillel was made Nasi for knowing a law no one else remembered, and then he scolded the leaders for being lazy. Minutes later he forgot a law himself. The Talmud draws the lesson: when a sage turns arrogant, his wisdom leaves him. Even Hillel had a bad moment.
passages.verbatim: Anyone who acts haughtily, if he is a Torah scholar, his wisdom departs from him

passages.text: When Hillel couldn't remember the law, he said: leave it to the people of Israel. If they aren't prophets, they are children of prophets. The next day they found the answer themselves, and Hillel recognized his teachers' tradition in what they did. Sometimes the people you teach already know.
passages.verbatim: But leave it to the Jewish people; if they are not prophets to whom God has revealed His secrets, they are the sons of prophets

passages.text: Hillel was walking home and heard a scream from the city. He said: I'm sure it isn't coming from my house. The Talmud applies the verse 'He shall not fear evil tidings; his heart is steady, trusting in God.'
passages.verbatim: I am certain that the scream is not coming from my house.

passages.text: A poor man from a noble family had lost everything, including the servant who used to run ahead of him. When Hillel couldn't find someone to run ahead of him, he ran ahead of him himself for three miles. He gave what that person was missing, not what was convenient to give.
passages.verbatim: Hillel himself ran in front of him for three mil

passages.text: Hillel saw that people stopped lending to the poor as the Sabbatical year approached, so he created the prozbul to keep loans flowing. He looked at how people actually behaved and changed the system so kindness was still possible.
passages.verbatim: he saw that the people of the nation were refraining from lending to one another

passages.ref: Tosefta Berakhot 2:22 (Sefaria numbering; 2:21 in some editions)
passages.text: Hillel said: don't stand when others sit or sit when others stand, don't laugh among those weeping or weep among those laughing. There is a time to weep and a time to laugh. Read the room you're in.

A heavenly voice said someone present was worthy of the Divine Presence like Moses, but his generation wasn't ready, and the sages looked at Hillel. When he died, they mourned him with the words: Alas, the pious one, alas, the humble one, a student of Ezra.
passages.verbatim: Alas, the pious man, alas, the humble man, a disciple of Ezra.

jonathan_sacks.label: Rabbi Jonathan Sacks
jonathan_sacks.work: Covenant & Conversation; The Dignity of Difference; To Heal a Fractured World; Lessons in Leadership
jonathan_sacks.bio: Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth (1991–2013) and a philosopher whose weekly Torah essays, Covenant & Conversation, brought Jewish thought to bear on leadership, education and life in a diverse society.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Bo, "Freedom's Defence" (a 'civilisation' variant appears in From Optimism to Hope, p. 131)
passages.text: To defend a country you need an army; but to defend a free society you need schools.
passages.verbatim: To defend a country, you need an army. But to defend a free society, you need schools.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Bo, "Freedom's Defence" (retelling Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah 1)
passages.text: Rabbi Judah the Prince sent rabbis to set up teachers in every town. In one town the people proudly showed them the armed guard, and the rabbis said: these are not the protectors of the town. The real guardians of a city are its teachers.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Devarim, "The Teacher as Hero"
passages.text: Told he would never enter the land, Moses could have spent his last month in disappointment. Instead he became a teacher, explaining not just what to do but why. Rabbi Sacks says it is teachers, not rulers or poets, who really shape a society.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Pinchas, "On Parents and Teachers"
passages.text: Aaron was succeeded by his son, Moses by his student Joshua. A parent passes the tradition to children, and a teacher passes it to disciples. The students who carry your teaching forward are your heirs too.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Devarim, "The Teacher as Hero" (on Deut. 1:5, be'er, 'to explain')
passages.text: Moses 'explained' the Torah: he gave reasons, rooted in what the people had lived through. Judaism is not a faith of mysteries for a few insiders. Good teaching makes the reason clear enough for anyone to own it.

passages.ref: The Dignity of Difference, p. 53 (as quoted on rabbisacks.org teaching resources)
passages.text: The miracle of monotheism is not one God, one truth, one way. It is that unity in heaven creates diversity on earth: God's oneness shows up in the variety of what God made, including the variety in your room.

passages.ref: The Dignity of Difference, pp. 100–101 (as quoted on rabbisacks.org teaching resources)
passages.text: Because we are different, what I lack someone else has, and what they lack I have. Difference is not a threat to be managed but the reason we need each other. When difference leads to conflict both sides lose; when it leads to exchange both gain.

passages.ref: The Dignity of Difference, p. 201 (as quoted on rabbisacks.org teaching resources)
passages.text: Rabbi Sacks asks the hard question of faith: can I recognise God's image in someone who is not in my image? The test is not loving people who are like us. It is seeing the divine face in the one who thinks, prays or behaves differently.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Masei, "Leadership at a Time of Crisis" (on Jeremiah 29:7)
passages.text: Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city they lived in and pray for it, because its peace would be their peace. Rabbi Sacks calls this the first statement of what it means to be a creative minority: keep your identity and give generously to the place you live.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Chayei Sarah, "The Kindness of Strangers" (from Stephen Carter, Civility)
passages.text: In 1966 a Black family moved onto a white street in Washington, and the neighbours walked past without a word. Then a woman crossed the street, welcomed the children, and brought them sandwiches. She was Sara Kestenbaum, a religious Jew, and one small act of kindness turned strangers into friends.

The Torah does not just say love the stranger; it says you know the stranger's heart, because you were strangers in Egypt. Reason alone does not defeat fear of the outsider. Memory does: you once stood where they stand now.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Yitro, "A Nation of Leaders" (on Exodus 18:17–22)
passages.text: Jethro watched Moses judging the people alone from morning to night and said: what you are doing is not good. The phrase 'not good' appears only one other time in the Torah, about being alone. We cannot lead alone; sharing the load is not weakness but wisdom.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Beha'alotecha, "Leadership Beyond Despair" (on Numbers 11:14)
passages.text: Even Moses broke down: I cannot carry all these people by myself; the burden is too heavy. Elijah, Jeremiah and Jonah felt the same. God's answer was not a lecture but seventy elders to share the weight, and the strength to go on.
Leadership in a noble cause can bring despair. But it also is the cure.
passages.verbatim: Leadership in a noble cause can bring despair. But it also is the cure.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Vayikra, "The Sins of a Leader" (on Leviticus 4:22)
passages.text: For the leader's sin offering the Torah says 'when' a leader sins, not 'if'. Mistakes come with leading. Leadership needs two kinds of courage: to take a risk, and to admit it when the risk fails. Happy the group whose leader can say 'I got that wrong.'
A leader is one who takes responsibility. Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent; Moses saw a wrong and stepped in when no one else would.
passages.verbatim: A leader is one who takes responsibility.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Nitzavim–Vayelech, "Leadership: Consensus or Command?"
passages.text: At the end of his life Moses saw that he had taken the Israelites out of Egypt but not Egypt out of the Israelites. Changing habits of mind takes far longer than changing circumstances, so he told Joshua to lead patiently and bring people along, even if it meant going slower.

passages.ref: To Heal a Fractured World, p. 166 (rabbisacks.org quotes)
passages.text: Optimism and hope are not the same. Optimism is believing things will get better; hope is believing that together we can make them better. It needs no courage to be an optimist, but it takes a great deal of courage to hope.
passages.verbatim: It needs no courage to be an optimist, but it takes a great deal of courage to hope.

passages.ref: "Optimism is all very well, but it takes courage to hope", The Times, 30 April 2010
passages.text: Faith, Rabbi Sacks wrote, is not wishful thinking. It means seeing the world exactly as it is and still refusing to stop believing it could be otherwise: realism touched by hope.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Tzav, "Giving Thanks" (on Modeh Ani)
passages.text: The first words a Jew says on waking are Modeh Ani, I give thanks, before any plan or worry about the day. We thank before we think. Gratitude first sets the tone for everything that follows.
passages.verbatim: We thank before we think.

passages.ref: Covenant & Conversation, Eikev, "The Power of Gratitude" (on Deuteronomy 8)
passages.text: Moses warned that the danger would come in good times, when people forget how they got where they are. Gratitude keeps us humble, reminding us how much we owe to others; Rabbi Sacks cites research linking it to health and resilience.

passages.ref: A Letter in the Scroll, p. 140 (rabbisacks.org Shabbat teaching resources)
passages.text: Rabbi Sacks described Shabbat as the day we stand still and let all our blessings catch up with us. A restless people found rest and renewal there. Stopping is not lost time; it is when you finally notice what you have.

rebbe_nachman.label: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov
rebbe_nachman.work: Likutei Moharan, Sichot HaRan, Sippurei Ma'asiyot
rebbe_nachman.bio: Hasidic master and great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov who led a small circle of followers in Breslov, Ukraine, and died in Uman at 38. His student Reb Noson recorded his teachings, conversations and tales, which center on joy, honest prayer in one's own words, and never giving up.

passages.text: When someone in front of you looks like nothing but trouble, go looking for the one small point of good in them, the place where they are not the problem. Rebbe Nachman taught that finding that point and judging them by it actually lifts them, and can turn them around.

Do the same for yourself. When you look at your day and see only failure, refuse to fall into gloom; keep searching until you find one good thing you did, even a flawed one, and let it revive you. Then look for the next one.

Rebbe Nachman said that gathering good points is how a melody is made, and that the one fit to lead a congregation in prayer is the one who can gather the good point in every person present. A teacher who collects the good in each student is doing the same work.

Set aside time each day, ideally an hour, alone in a room or a field, and simply talk to God in your own language. Say everything that is in your heart, the regrets and the hopes, the way you would speak to a close friend.
If you sit down to speak and no words come, that is still good: your being there and wanting to speak counts. You can even make that your prayer, asking simply to be able to open your mouth.

Rebbe Nachman said that every great tzaddik reached what they reached through hitbodedut, private conversation with God, and that it is open to everyone, from the least to the greatest. You do not need special standing to begin; you need a few honest minutes.
It is a great mitzvah to be happy always, and to work hard at keeping sadness and gloom away.
passages.verbatim: It is a great mitzvah to always be happy, and to make every effort to determinedly keep depression and gloom at bay.

passages.text: Human nature drifts toward gloom, and everyone carries some suffering, so joy takes real effort, even a bit of silliness if that is what it takes. Give remorse its own short, set time in the day, and spend the rest of the day in joy.

A person has to cross a very, very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid at all. (The popular song by Rabbi Baruch Chait reworks this as "the whole world is a very narrow bridge"; the original speaks of a person crossing it, with a doubled "very".)
passages.verbatim: Know, too! a person must cross a very, very narrow bridge. The main rule is: Do not be frightened at all!

passages.text: Rebbe Nachman taught that when you start to serve God and feel pushed away at every turn, the truth is that every distancing is really a way of being drawn closer.
passages.verbatim: In reality, all distancing is nothing but being brought near.

passages.text: Even the smallest move away from what weighs you down and toward what matters is enormous; Rebbe Nachman said that a tiny shift down here covers thousands of miles above. And those small movements gather together and come to help you when you need them most.
Be stubborn about the good you have started. Hold your place, even the little bit of progress you have made, no matter what knocks you down, and even if you fall again and again.
There is no despair in the world at all. Reb Noson records that Rebbe Nachman said it in Yiddish, drawing out the words with great force: Kein yiush iz gor nit fahr-handin.
passages.verbatim: there is no such thing as despair!

passages.text: On not despairing over the damage you have done, Rebbe Nachman said: if you believe you can ruin things, believe you can fix them.
passages.verbatim: If you believe it is possible to destroy, believe it is possible to repair!

passages.text: Think only about today. Seen as a whole lifetime, the work feels impossible, but when you only have this day, it is no burden at all; and do not put off till tomorrow, because tomorrow is a whole different world.
passages.verbatim: For a person’s world consists only of the present day and moment—tomorrow is a different world entirely.

passages.text: Reb Noson recalls that as a boy, Rebbe Nachman would resolve to serve God fully, slip, and begin again, many times in a single day. That was his rule: whenever you fall, start over as if you were just beginning.
passages.verbatim: No matter how many times you fall, rise up and start again.

passages.text: Rebbe Nachman called the ability to forget a gift: if we remembered everything, the past would drag us down. Once something is finished, put it out of your mind and come to the next moment fresh.

Workers were hired to fill leaky barrels. The foolish ones complained that it all ran out; the wise ones said, we are paid by the day, so what does it matter? Rebbe Nachman said learning is like that: even what is forgotten is not wasted.

Do as much good as you can, but do not panic over everything you have not done. Go slowly, one step at a time; Rebbe Nachman said that people rushing out of a burning house often save the most worthless things.
Rebbe Nachman often said that serving God needs no sophistication, only simplicity, sincerity and faith, and that simplicity is the highest thing there is.
passages.verbatim: The Rebbe said that simplicity is the highest possible thing.

passages.text: Rebbe Nachman said his own achievements came mainly through simplicity: plain conversation with God and saying Psalms. He would sigh, "Ay, prostik!" longing for the artless faith of ordinary people, and taught that cleverness is unnecessary; faith and straightforwardness are enough.

When you pray in a field, every plant joins in and strengthens your prayer; that is why prayer is called sichah, from siach ha-sadeh, the shrub of the field. Even indoors, the things around you help. Step outside when you can.

Every shepherd has his own melody, shaped by the grasses and the place where he pastures, because each blade of grass has its own song. A teacher's voice, too, grows out of the particular students in front of them.
Make a habit of lifting yourself with a melody. Even if you do not sing well, sing to yourself at home or alone; Rebbe Nachman said the power of melody is beyond measure.
Someone may be carrying pain with no one to tell it to. Rebbe Nachman said that coming to such a person with a happy face can literally give them life, and that this is no small thing.
passages.verbatim: If you come to such a person with a happy face, you can literally give him life.

passages.ref: Kokhavei Or, Sippurim Nifla'im (the Turkey Prince)
passages.text: A prince decided he was a turkey and sat naked under the table pecking at crumbs. A sage took off his own clothes and joined him, and once they were friends, he showed the prince that a turkey can wear a shirt, then pants, eat real food, and sit at the table, until the prince was healed. Meet a student where he is, and bring him up one step at a time.

A viceroy searched for years for the king's lost daughter. Twice he came within a day of freeing her and failed, once by eating an apple and falling asleep for years; each time he wept and kept searching. The tale ends: how he freed her, he did not tell, but in the end he freed her.
passages.verbatim: (And how he took her out, he did not tell.) (But) in the end, he took her out.

passages.text: A king handing his kingdom to his son tells him that the stars say he will one day fall from power, and asks only this: when you fall, do not be sad, be happy. If you cannot keep yourself happy, you are not fit to be king.

passages.ref: Sippurei Ma'asiyot 13 (The Seven Beggars), third day
passages.text: The heart of the world stands at one end of the world longing for a spring on a mountain at the other end. It can never go to the spring, because if it came closer it would lose sight of the peak, and it lives only by looking. So it stands and longs, and that longing keeps the whole world alive.

passages.ref: Sippurei Ma'asiyot 9 (The Clever Man and the Simple Man)
passages.text: The simple cobbler made poor shoes and lived on dry bread, yet he was always joyful, tasting every dish he wished for in his bread. When people mocked him, he would answer that if they were cleverer than him, that only made them the bigger fools.
passages.verbatim: So what if you are more clever than me? Would you not then be the real fool?
